summary: Derived the minimal data model the approved Counter plan requires: one new table, public.counter, holding a single row pinned by `check (id = 1)` with `value integer not null default 0` and `updated_at timestamptz not null default now()`. RLS is enabled with exactly one policy — counter_select_public (select, using true) — and deliberately no insert/update/delete policy, so the table is default-deny for writes and the only mutation path is the plan's SECURITY DEFINER `increment_counter()` function. No index beyond the primary key, since no policy or query filters on a non-key column. The already-applied `items` table from supabase/migrations/20260726000000_rls_baseline.sql is intentionally not restated. This artifact can express only tables, constraints, indexes, and RLS, so the increment function, its grants, and the seeded `(1, 0)` row are not covered here and remain plan task T1's responsibility; that gap is recorded in risks and nextActions.

decisions.title: One singleton row pinned by a check constraint instead of a multi-row counters table
decisions.choice: public.counter has `id integer primary key default 1` plus `check (id = 1)`, so the table can hold at most one row, which is the counter.
decisions.rationale: The PRD declares one Counter entity with one integer value and excludes multiple counters, auth, and history. The check constraint makes "there is exactly one counter" a database invariant rather than an application convention, so no code path can create a second counter or read the wrong one.
alternatives: A table keyed by a text `name` column with a unique constraint (allows multiple counters — excluded by the PRD)
An append-only events table aggregated with sum() (this is the history of changes the PRD excludes)
A single-row table with no check constraint (a stray insert silently produces two counters and an ambiguous read)
consequences: Reads can use `where id = 1` or `limit 1` interchangeably; both are guaranteed to address the same row.
The check constraint guarantees at most one row but cannot guarantee the row exists — the insert of `(1, 0)` still has to happen in the migration.
Adding a second counter later requires a forward migration dropping the check constraint.

decisions.title: RLS enabled with a select-only policy and no write policy
decisions.choice: `alter table public.counter enable row level security` plus exactly one policy, counter_select_public, for select with `using (true)`; no insert, update, or delete policy is declared.
decisions.rationale: The PRD excludes auth, so there is no auth.uid() to scope rows to and a public read is the intended behavior. Omitting write policies leaves the table default-deny for every direct write, which keeps the anon key from setting an arbitrary value while the plan's SECURITY DEFINER increment function — which bypasses RLS — remains the only way the number can change, and it can only add one.
alternatives: An anon update policy with `using (true) with check (true)`, letting any caller PATCH the counter to any value
Policies restricted `to authenticated`, which would make the page require a sign-in the PRD's non-goals forbid
Leaving RLS disabled, which the harness forbids and which would expose the table to unrestricted anon writes
consequences: Any caller, signed in or not, can read the current value; that is the intended product behavior for a public counter.
A direct PATCH/POST/DELETE against /rest/v1/counter with the anon key affects zero rows, which is the acceptance check stated in plan task T1.
Because the policy is declared without an explicit role clause it applies to `public`, covering both anon and authenticated as the plan's `to anon, authenticated` intended.

decisions.title: updated_at, and deliberately no created_at
decisions.choice: The table carries `updated_at timestamptz not null default now()` and no created_at column.
decisions.rationale: The approved plan specifies updated_at and has increment_counter() set it, giving a cheap record of last activity. created_at is omitted on purpose: scripts/database-row-match.mjs identifies browser-created rows on tables that have a created_at column, and the singleton counter row is created by the migration, not by a browser action, so a created_at column would invite a false match.
alternatives: Add created_at for symmetry with public.items (risks a false browser-row match and records nothing useful for a row created by a migration)
Drop updated_at as well, for the strictly smallest table (loses the last-increment timestamp the approved plan asked for)
consequences: Nothing in the plan reads updated_at; it exists for operability, and the increment function is responsible for maintaining it.
scripts/database-row-match.mjs will not treat the counter row as browser-created, so plan task T5/T7 acceptance rests on the rendered count and the post-reload value, as the plan already states.

decisions.title: The existing items table is not restated in this schema plan
decisions.choice: This artifact declares only public.counter. public.items, created by the already-applied supabase/migrations/20260726000000_rls_baseline.sql, is left out.
decisions.rationale: Migrations are forward-only and the baseline is already applied. A generated schema-plan migration that re-declared items would fail with "relation public.items already exists" and block every downstream task. The approved plan changes nothing about items — it only moves the page that renders them from / to /items.
alternatives: Restate items so the artifact describes the full database (breaks the generated migration)
Drop and recreate items to fold it into this plan (destroys the seeded rows that browser-tests/cross-tenant-denial.json depends on)
consequences: This artifact is the delta for this plan, not a full inventory of the database.
items keeps its four owner-scoped policies and its items_user_id_idx index untouched, so pnpm smoke and the cross-tenant browser test are unaffected.

assumptions: Tables in this artifact live in the `public` schema; "counter" means public.counter, matching the baseline migration's convention.

The counter is one globally shared value, per the approved plan's default for its open question Q1. If the operator answers "one counter per browser" instead, this schema is wrong: it would need a visitor-identifier column, an index on it, and visitor-scoped policies.
A 32-bit `integer` is sufficient for the value; the PRD sets no ceiling and defines no overflow behavior.

`id` is declared `integer` rather than the `smallint` named in the approved plan's T1 deliverable, because this artifact's column-type vocabulary has no smallint. The behavior is identical for a value pinned to 1; only the on-disk width differs.
A policy declared without an explicit role clause applies to the `public` role, which covers both anon and authenticated — the coverage the approved plan expressed as `to anon, authenticated`.

The generated supabase/migrations/<timestamp>_schema_plan.sql will contain the create table, its constraints, `enable row level security`, and the one policy above, and nothing else, since this artifact has no field for functions, grants, or data.
risks: This artifact cannot express functions, grants, or seed data, so the generated schema-plan migration will create an empty, unwritable counter table. Until plan task T1 adds `public.increment_counter()` with its grants and inserts the `(1, 0)` row, `GET /counter` returns zero rows rather than `{"value": 0}` and there is no write path at all. If T1 is dropped as "already covered by the schema plan", the feature cannot work.

The `(1, 0)` row must be inserted by a migration, not by supabase/seed.sql. seed.sql is local-development data that a deployed stack never applies, and the app has no insert path (no insert policy, and the increment function only updates), so a counter row seeded only in seed.sql leaves a deployed stack permanently empty.

The counter is world-readable and — through the anon execute grant on the increment function — world-incrementable. That is inherent to a no-auth PRD, and rate limiting is out of scope, so the value is not trustworthy as a metric.

`check (id = 1)` bounds the table to at most one row but does not guarantee the row exists. There is no delete policy, so no anon or authenticated caller can remove it, but a service-role or superuser delete would leave `update ... where id = 1 returning value` matching zero rows and the increment silently returning null.

The increment function the plan depends on is SECURITY DEFINER. Omitting `set search_path = ''` on it is a real privilege-escalation weakness that no check in this workspace catches, and it sits in T1, outside this artifact's surface.

`value` is int4, so the counter overflows at 2,147,483,647 and errors rather than wrapping. For a toy counter that is unreachable, but the schema encodes no ceiling and the PRD defines no overflow behavior.
nextActions: Narrow plan task T1 to exactly what this schema plan does not cover: `create function public.increment_counter() returns integer language sql security definer set search_path = ''` performing `update public.counter set value = value + 1, updated_at = now() where id = 1 returning value`, then `revoke all on function public.increment_counter() from public` and `grant execute ... to anon, authenticated`. T1 must not redeclare the table, its constraints, RLS, or the counter_select_public policy.

Include `insert into public.counter (id, value) values (1, 0) on conflict (id) do nothing;` in that same T1 migration — not in supabase/seed.sql — so the row exists in every environment and `pnpm db:reset` is idempotent.

Run `pnpm db:types` (plan task T2) only after both the generated schema-plan migration and T1's function migration are applied, so apps/api/src/database.types.ts carries both public.Tables.counter and public.Functions.increment_counter in one regeneration.

Verify the schema-plan migration's policy is emitted for the `public` role (or explicitly `to anon, authenticated`). If the generator instead scopes policies to `authenticated`, the anonymous read the PRD requires fails and T1 must add the anon-visible select policy.
